issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not interfere with an interlocutory order unless the order would finally dispose of the proceeding or, if left in force, would cause a failure of justice or irreparable injury.
material_facts: A party sought the trial judge’s voluntary transfer of a pending civil suit, and the judge dismissed that request and listed another pending application for orders.
The party challenged the dismissal in revision, and the High Court stayed the trial proceedings.
The challenged order would not have finally disposed of the suit, and the party’s inability to obtain an adjournment arose from its counsel’s decision to abstain from the court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court lacked jurisdiction to entertain the revision because neither statutory exception to the restriction on revisional interference applied; the revisional proceedings were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, inserted by the 1976 amendment, bars revision of an order made in the course of a suit or other proceeding unless the order would finally dispose of the proceeding or, if allowed to stand, would cause a failure of justice or irreparable injury. Ram Lal v. Madan Gopal was distinguishable: it concerned a party denied the opportunity to make oral submissions, and its course of action was expressly based on the special facts of that case.

rule.if: revision_challenges_interlocutory_order and not order_would_end_proceeding and not order_would_cause_failure_of_justice_or_irreparable_injury

predicates.revision_challenges_interlocutory_order: A party seeks revision of an order made during an ongoing suit or other proceeding.
predicates.order_would_end_proceeding: The challenged order, if made in favour of the applicant, would finally dispose of the proceeding.
predicates.order_would_cause_failure_of_justice_or_: The challenged order, if left in force, would cause a failure of justice or irreparable injury to the party challenging it.
predicates.high_court_must_not_interfere_in_revisio: The High Court does not interfere with the challenged order in revision.

issues.definition: When a revision challenges an interlocutory order that would neither end the proceeding nor cause a failure of justice or irreparable injury, the High Court must not interfere in revision.

issues.legal_issue: An advocate’s boycott or deliberate absence does not require a court to adjourn a matter, and an advocate who retains a client’s brief while abstaining from the court cannot use the resulting absence to obstruct the judicial process.
material_facts: The respondent’s counsel retained the brief but did not attend the hearing, relying on a bar association’s boycott of the court.
The respondent also did not appear personally and sought a transfer or adjournment because of the boycott.
The trial judge dismissed the transfer request and proceeded with the pending matter.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was not required to adjourn the matter because of the boycott; it was entitled and obliged to proceed with its judicial business.
issues.legal_principle: Courts must conduct judicial business without yielding to boycott calls, pressure tactics or browbeating. An advocate who accepts a brief has a duty to attend the trial; failure to attend breaches professional duty, as stated in Lt. Col. S.J. Chaudhary v. State (Delhi Administration). If counsel does not wish to appear in a court, professional decorum requires giving up the engagement so the client can retain another advocate. High Courts are duty bound to protect judicial functionaries from intimidation.

predicates.court_is_hearing_pending_matter: A court is hearing a matter that is pending before it.
predicates.counsel_absents_from_court_due_to_boycot: An advocate does not attend the court because of a boycott call or decision to abstain from that court.
predicates.counsel_retains_client_brief: The advocate continues to hold the client’s brief while abstaining from the court.
predicates.court_must_continue_judicial_business_wi: The court continues its judicial business and does not adjourn the matter merely because of the boycott.

issues.definition: When a court is hearing a pending matter and counsel abstains because of a boycott while retaining the client’s brief, the court must continue its judicial business without an adjournment based on the boycott.

issues.legal_issue: The parties’ agreement to transfer a pending case, without an independent valid ground for transfer, is insufficient to justify changing the court hearing the case.
material_facts: The respondent asked for the suit to be transferred to another court after the dispute concerning the boycott and the trial judge’s refusal to transfer it.
The appellant stated that he had no objection to a transfer.
The Court found no valid ground for changing courts and considered that allowing transfer on consent alone could enable parties to choose their own court.
issues.conclusion: The request to transfer the suit was refused because the parties’ consent, without a valid ground for transfer, did not justify changing courts.
issues.legal_principle: Consent by both parties is not by itself a valid ground for changing the court hearing a case; otherwise, parties could combine to avoid one court and choose another. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

rule.if: civil_case_is_pending_before_court and transfer_is_requested and both_parties_consent and not independent_valid_transfer_ground_exists

predicates.civil_case_is_pending_before_court: A civil case is pending before a court.
predicates.transfer_is_requested: A party asks for the pending case to be heard by a different court.
predicates.both_parties_consent: Both parties agree to the requested change of court.
predicates.independent_valid_transfer_ground_exists: A valid ground for changing the court exists apart from the parties’ consent.
predicates.court_must_not_transfer_case_merely_on_p: The court does not transfer the case solely because both parties agree to the transfer.

issues.definition: If a civil case is pending, transfer is requested, both parties consent, and no independent valid ground exists, the court must not transfer the case merely on the basis of consent.
